title_en: The Presence of the Devils at the Deathbed
body_ar:
يذكر أن الشياطين تحضر الميت عند موته و تتمثل له في صورة أبويه فهل ذلك حق؟ النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أمرنا أن نستعيذ بالله من فتنة المحيا و الممات فقال: فاستعذ بالله من أربع قل اللهم إني أعوذ بك من عذاب القبر و من فتنة القبر و من فتنة المسيح الدجال و من فتنة المحيا و الممات فهذه الأربع يستعاذ بالله منها و في الرواية الأخرى اللهم إني أعوذ بك من عذاب جهنم و أعوذ بك من عذاب القبر و أعوذ بك من فتنة المسيح الدجال و أعوذ بك من فتنة المحيا و الممات هذه الأربعة يستعاذ بالله منها و منها فتنة المحيا و فتنة الممات ففتنة المحيا ما يعرض للإنسان في حياته من السراء و الضراء فالسراء تطغيه و الضراء تنسيه (إن الإنسان ليطغى أن رآه استغنى)

هل تنتظرون إلا غنى مطغيا أو فقرا منسيا و فتنة الممات هي الفتنة عند الموت و قد جاء فيها عدد من الأحاديث أن المحتضر الذي يفتن يعرض له الفتان فيقول: له مت على دين اليهودية مت على دين النصرانية و قد أخبرني أحد كبار العلماء في هذه البلاد أو سمعت منه ذلك و هو العلامة محمد عال و لد نعمة رحمة الله عليه أنه و قع مرة فمكث على جنبه فترة طويلة و أيقن على الموت حتى عرض له الفتان فكان يقول له مت على دين اليهودية مت على دين النصرانية و هو يكذبه و يجزره و برئ من ذلك المرض و عاش بعده فالفتان أيضا لا يعلم الغيب و تعرض الفتنة و قد تكون هذه الفتنة تظهر لبعض الناس إقامة للحجة على الناس و بيان لبعض الأمور التي هي غيبية فيكشفها الله لبعض خواصه من خلقه لزيادة الإيمان و لذلك حصل لعبد الله بن جحش رضي الله عنه أن أخته حمنة لما مرض كانت تناديه فتقول واجبلاه واطوداه فلما أفاق قال: ما قلت شيئا إلا قيل لي أهكذا كنت فلما قتل يوم أحد لم تبك عليه و كذلك فهذا النوع من الفتنة عند الموت عرض لأحمد بن حنبل رحمه الله تعالى فقد صح عن ابنه صالح أنه قال: حضرت أبا عبد الله عند موته فإذا هو يقول لا بعد لا بعد فقلت يا أبتي ما ذا تقول قال إن عدو الله عرض لي و هو يقول فتني يا أحمد و أنا أقول لا بعد حتى أموت على الإيمان عدو الله الشيطان عرض له و يقول فتني يا أحمد يريد أن يدخل عليه العجب في آخر ساعة من حياته.
body_en:
It is said that the devils are present with a dying person at his death and take on for him the form of his parents. Is that true?

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded us to seek refuge with God from the trial of life and of death. He said: 'Seek refuge with God from four. Say: O God, I seek refuge with You from the punishment of the grave, and from the trial of the grave, and from the trial of the Antichrist (al-Masīḥ al-Dajjāl), and from the trial of life and of death.' These four are what refuge is sought from with God. And in the other transmission: 'O God, I seek refuge with You from the punishment of Hell, and I seek refuge with You from the punishment of the grave, and I seek refuge with You from the trial of the Antichrist, and I seek refuge with You from the trial of life and of death.' These four are what refuge is sought from with God, and among them are the trial of life and the trial of death. The trial of life is what befalls a person in his lifetime of ease and of hardship: ease drives him to transgress and hardship makes him forget. {Truly man transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient} (Sūrat al-ʿAlaq 96:6–7).

'Are you waiting for anything but a wealth that makes you transgress, or a poverty that makes you forget?' The trial of death is the trial at the moment of dying. A number of reports have come about it: that the dying person who is put to the trial has the tempter (al-fattān) present himself to him, saying to him: Die upon the religion of Judaism! Die upon the religion of Christianity! One of the great scholars of this country told me — or rather I heard it from him — and that is the erudite Muhammad ʿAl wuld Niʿmah, God's mercy upon him, that he once fell ill and remained lying on his side for a long period and was certain of death, until the tempter presented himself to him and kept saying to him: Die upon the religion of Judaism! Die upon the religion of Christianity! — while he gave him the lie and drove him off. And he recovered from that illness and lived on after it. So the tempter, too, does not know the unseen; he simply presents the trial. This trial may be made visible to some people as a way of establishing the proof against people, and of making plain some of the matters that belong to the unseen, which God discloses to some of the select among His creation so that faith may increase. That is why it happened to ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, God be pleased with him, that when he was ill his sister Hamnah would call out to him, saying: 'O my mountain! O my great peak!' — and when he came to, he said: 'You said nothing but that it was said to me, Were you really such?' And so when he was killed on the day of Uhud she did not weep for him. Likewise this kind of trial at death befell Ahmad ibn Hanbal, God the exalted have mercy on him. It is soundly established from his son Salih that he said: I was present with Abu ʿAbd Allah at his death, and there he was saying: 'Not yet, not yet.' I said: Father, what are you saying? He said: The enemy of God presented himself to me, and he was saying: You have got the better of me, Ahmad! — and I was saying: Not yet, not until I die upon faith. The enemy of God — Satan — presented himself to him and was saying: You have got the better of me, Ahmad! — wanting to bring self-admiration upon him in the last hour of his life.

flags.context: Satan's words to Ahmad ibn Hanbal at his death, and Ahmad's reply لا بعد
options: 'You have got the better of me, Ahmad!' — reading فُتَّنِي, with لا بعد as 'not yet'
'Tempt me, Ahmad!' — reading فتِّنِّي as an imperative
flags.note: This is the most uncertain rendering in the record and it changes the sense of the whole anecdote. The well-known transmission of Salih's account has Satan biting his fingers and saying fittanī yā Aḥmad — conventionally understood as Satan conceding that Ahmad has escaped him — and Ahmad replying lā baʿd, 'not yet', i.e. not until I die upon faith. The Sheikh's own closing gloss supports that reading: he says Satan wanted to bring ʿujb, self-admiration, upon Ahmad in his last hour, which only works if Satan is flattering him with a concession. But the Arabic as printed here is unvowelled and could be read as an imperative. Flagged for the Sheikh's office rather than resolved.

flags.arabic: مت على دين اليهودية مت على دين النصرانية
flags.context: the words the Sheikh reports the tempter as saying to the dying person, repeated twice in the record
options: render literally, as the words of the tempter, with the attribution unmistakable
render with an added editorial frame
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW. The line names two religious communities and is repeated twice. In the Arabic it is unambiguously placed in the mouth of Satan as a temptation to apostasy, and the Sheikh is not characterising Judaism or Christianity here at all. Lifted out of the record in English it will read very differently. Translated faithfully, with the attribution kept explicit in both occurrences; the decision on whether and how to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.context: the scholar's response to the tempter
options: 'while he gave him the lie and drove him off' — reading يزجره
'while he gave him the lie and cut him short' — reading يجزره as from jazara
leave the second verb untranslated and mark it as illegible
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT. يجزره is very probably a metathesis of يزجره, yazjuruhu, 'rebukes/drives him off', which pairs naturally with yukadhdhibuhu. The source spelling is preserved in body_ar per the house rule against silently fixing the source; the English takes the likely reading and flags it.

flags.arabic: هل تنتظرون إلا غنى مطغيا أو فقرا منسيا
flags.context: quoted immediately after the Qur'anic verse, with no introduction
options: render as a quotation from the Prophet, as the context implies
render as continuing the Sheikh's own voice
render and mark the speaker as unidentified
flags.note: The source gives this with no introduction, no speaker, no narrator and no grading, running straight on from the Qur'anic verse in a new paragraph. It is in fact part of a well-known prophetic report, but the Sheikh does not say so here, so nothing has been supplied. The English keeps it in quotation marks without attributing it, which leaves the reader where the Arabic leaves them. A reviewer should decide whether the site identifies it.

flags.arabic: يذكر أن الشياطين تحضر الميت عند موته و تتمثل له في صورة أبويه فهل ذلك حق؟
flags.context: the question asked, set against the answer given
options: render faithfully and mark that the specific claim is not ruled on
present the answer as confirming the claim
present the answer as denying it
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. The question asks specifically whether the devils take on the form of the dying person's parents. The Sheikh never addresses that detail. He establishes that there is a trial at death and that a tempter presents himself, and gives three accounts of it — but in none of them does the tempter appear in the form of a parent. A reader will take the answer for a yes, and the site must not present it as one.

translator_notes: The date carried here is the CMS record date. Across this whole slice the site serves a bulk-upload timestamp of 19-21 December 2010, which is when the written archive was loaded into the site, not when the Sheikh gave the answer or delivered the lecture. date_is_cms_upload is set true. The real date of composition is not recoverable from the page and has not been guessed.
Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The Qur'anic quotation is given in the source in round brackets and without a reference; the reference has been supplied per house style. The wording matches Sūrat al-ʿAlaq 96:6–7.

The two prophetic supplications are given by the Sheikh without narrator, collection or grading; he distinguishes them only as 'the other transmission'. Nothing has been supplied. These are recited formulae, so the Arabic in body_ar is the operative text.

Muhammad ʿAl wuld Niʿmah is a Mauritanian scholar of the Sheikh's own milieu; the name is romanised as the Arabic gives it. A reviewer may wish to fix a standard romanisation of the Mauritanian patronymic 'wuld'.
'O my mountain! O my great peak!' renders wā jabalāh, wā ṭawdāh, the conventional cries of lamentation; the Arabic is an idiom of mourning and has no close English equivalent.
The Sheikh says of the account from Salih ibn Ahmad that it is soundly established (ṣaḥīḥ); that grading is his and has been kept. He gives no grading for anything else in the record.
